newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Gulf tensions, Mexican blast fuel Asia LPG prices.
newsitem.headline: Gulf tensions, Mexican blast fuel Asia LPG prices.

text.p: Liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) prices in Asia are soaring as Gulf tensions add to worries over tight supplies caused by a Mexican gas-plant blast earlier this year, industry sources said on Monday.
In Japan and the Middle East, premiums over the contract price, the Middle East benchmark price for LPG, have risen by at least $10 per tonne since early August, Asian traders said.
In China, premiums in Shanghai have doubled to $80 per tonne from $35-$40 in August, traders in Shanghai and Hong Kong said.
Prices have firmed as less LPG heads to Asia from the Middle East, particularly from Saudi Arabia.
More supplies from the Gulf have been diverted to North America following a crippling explosion at state-run Pemex's biggest gas processing plant on July 26, they said.
Mexico signed a contract with Saudi Arabia to buy 240,000 to 250,000 tonnes of LPG for delivery between September and March.
Production levels at the Pemex plant will not recover until next June, company sources said recently.
While the blast sparked a quick surge in U.S. prices, Far East -- and especially Chinese -- buyers felt the impact only recently, Asian traders said.
Most of the floating storage tankers anchored along the southern coast of China are replenished with spot-market supplies from the Middle East, a Hong Kong trader said.

"They are due for replenishment and fresh supplies, if any, will only arrive at the end of this month," one trader said. "The supply disruption at Pemex would probably still be felt for a while until production resumes."
Traders said U.S.-Iraqi tensions also had fuelled firmer prices. As Iraq fired missiles at U.S. warplanes and Washington retaliated, Gulf suppliers held back on spot sales.
"We will probably see lower-than-normal Mideast supplies heading towards the Far East later this month," the Hong Kong trader said.
Traders said situation was further aggravated by buyers, worried over supply security in the Middle East, scrambling for cargoes in the past three weeks.
Japanese buyers were less concerned as more than 90 percent of their imports are on term contracts, but buyers in China import most of their supplies on a spot basis, traders said.
To add to buyers' woes, South Korean sellers, expecting further price gains, are withholding spot supplies, a Chinese buyer in Zhuhai in southern China told Reuters.
He said Chinese buyers were hopeful that prices would ease by the end of September, since the floating storage tankers off southern China were expecting supplies from the Middle East.
But any price fall, assuming U.S.-Iraqi tensions ease, was likely to be only temporary with the beginning of winter demand pushing them back up again, traders said.
